result:
No — don't cut production over this week. Here's why, and what would actually let you proceed.

**The problem:** everything you have — "99.9% accuracy," "SOC2 compliant," "enterprise-grade safety," case studies — is vendor marketing, not evidence from your own testing. None of it has been independently verified against your traffic, your content categories, or your failure tolerance.

**Critical characteristics your use relies on** (for a moderation API, at minimum):
- **Accuracy/recall on your actual content mix** — the vendor's "99.9%" is on their benchmark, not yours. Moderation false negatives (missed abuse/CSAM/harassment) are a materially different risk than false positives.
- **SOC2 report itself, not the badge** — "SOC2 compliant" means nothing until you've read the actual report (Type I vs II, which trust criteria, any exceptions noted).
- **Latency/availability under your load**
- **API/response format stability** — will their categories and confidence scores map cleanly to your existing moderation logic?
- **Data handling** — what happens to the content you send them (retention, training use, subprocessors)? This matters especially if you're sending user-generated content to a third party.

**Gaps right now:** all of the above are unverified. Case studies are someone else's use case, not proof for yours. This blocks acceptance for production use — not because the vendor is necessarily bad, but because you have no repo-side evidence yet.

**What would unblock it:**
1. Request the actual SOC2 report (ask for Type II if you're handling sensitive/user data) and read it — don't accept the badge as proof.
2. Run it in shadow mode against your production traffic for a period, comparing its decisions to your current pipeline, and eyeball the disagreements — especially false negatives on your most sensitive categories.
3. Get contractual terms on data retention/use in writing.
4. Confirm SLA/latency under realistic load.

**Backup control if you're time-pressured on cost:** run it in parallel/shadow alongside your existing provider rather than cutting over, so you get pricing pressure relief data without swapping the safety-critical decision-maker blind.

**Re-check trigger going forward:** any model/version update on their side, since a vendor swapping their underlying model resets whatever track record you build.

This is a security/safety-adjacent decision (content moderation failures have real user-harm and liability consequences), so if you do proceed, loop in whoever owns trust & safety or security review before go-live — this isn't a call to make on pricing alone.
